segments.text: I know when it started. It was in Greece-- the country, not the musical. I spent part of my childhood there. I was six or seven years old when I found a two-disk CD set at the bottom of some sales bin, a best of Broadway compilation from various European tours of Broadway shows, all in different languages. I remember a German "I Am What I Am" from "La Cage aux Folles."

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: [MUSIC - "I AM WHAT I AM']

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: [NON-ENGLISH SINGING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I listened over and over, arms outstretched, pretending I was onstage, spotlit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [NON-ENGLISH SINGING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It only escalated from there. Back in America, in my bedroom in Virginia, I Scotch-taped up pictures of Ethel Merman, Bernadette Peters, Bebe Neuwirth. On weekends, I checked casting calls in the Washington Post. My mom's rule was if an audition was less than five miles away, I could try out. I recorded the Tonys on VHS each year, watched it over and over.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Same for "Sound Of Music" and "Fiddler on the Roof." But the tape I watched the most, the one that spoke to me more than any other, was this 1997 TV special. Barbara Walters hosted, and it was called "Broadway's New Annie: Search For A Star." and if the title doesn't give it away, here's the premise. The musical "Annie" was coming back to Broadway and the show's director needed to find a star. And this was how he decided to do it, on TV.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Little girls, little girls, 2,000 little girls all sharing the same dream.

segments.speaker: Girl
segments.text: Annie, Annie, Annie, Annie, Annie.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: I was 8, the same age as those girls. I could have auditioned if I'd known about it. It was a nationwide contest sponsored by the department store Macy's, and there was a Macy's less than five miles from my house. To watch, I dressed up like an orphan, and the closest thing I came up with was wearing my older brother's underwear.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: I'd stand in front of the TV transfixed, so close my mom would yell at me that I was going to damage my eyes. And the person I was watching for was this one girl named Harley who reminded me of me because she was special, perfect for the role in every way, which I figured I'd be. Although Harley had the advantage of also looking the part-- long red wavy hair, chubby cheeks. The sort of aw, shucks grin you want to see on Annie's face. Except.

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: But then, it was Harley's turn to sing.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: (SINGING) Tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Martin Charnin
segments.text: I don't want you to do that. You're going tomorrow, tomorrow. Tomorrow! Too! Loud! (SINGING) Too.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: (SINGING) Too.

segments.speaker: Martin Charnin
segments.text: Too. Too. Too! Too!

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: Just sometimes, I get kind of scared, and it was really scary. So it kind of like came out.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: She's scared, which is kind of understandable. The guy she's auditioning for is Martin Charnin. He wrote "Annie" back in 1976. He was the show's original director. That's him you hear singing along with her. Martin takes Harley by the hand, and leads her away from all the other girls.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: He cups her chin in his palm, and places her on the floor by his feet, and together they watch more Annie hopefuls audition.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: Then I sat with the director, and then he let me watch.

segments.speaker: Martin Charnin
segments.text: So 149 was singing with you, right?

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: Something about the little girl's face makes Martin want to see her again. She makes the finals.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: I'm just going to think about just smile, and do your best.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: I loved this story because Harley just needed to be noticed by the right person, just like I needed.

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: August 7, at a nondescript rehearsal hall in Midtown Manhattan, the finalists have gathered selected from 2,000 of the last auditions. Harley Ott, one of Martin's favorites, is back from Jersey. She has another chance to sing, but again is struck with stage fright.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: (SINGING) You're always a day [INAUDIBLE].

segments.text: Day a-

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: A-

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: It doesn't go well, and still, later that day she gets a third chance.

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: Martin, who thinks she might be right for the role of an orphan, still believes he could overcome her nerves in rehearsal.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: OK, so now she's out of the running for Annie. But she may become an orphan on Broadway-- the kind of thing I'd have died for. As far as I was concerned, Harley had made it. But then comes the moment I haven't been able to understand for more than 20 years. As a kid I found it upsetting, as an adult baffling. Martin walks into the hall to grab Harley.

segments.speaker: Martin Charnin
segments.text: Is Harley here?

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: But when he goes to find her parents.

segments.speaker: Martin Charnin
segments.text: Brian, where did Harley's parents go?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I had them right in that chair, right here all three of them.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: He finds they've left.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: On screen, you see a confused Martin looking around anxiously. He's still not done with her, still picturing her in his cast list, but she was gone. For a moment, he stands there probably thinking exactly what I'm thinking.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: Why the hell would you ever walk out on that? Harley threw away her shot, and ever since I've wondered why. So I tracked her down. She was really surprised to hear from me. It was so long ago, she said, but she was also totally game to talk. Harley and I actually have a lot in common.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: We're both from the East Coast, we're both 30 years old, born just 10 days apart. She remembers everything about the audition.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: And then I remember these, like, boards we had to walk under. It was like you had to be under a certain height to even go into the audition, cause you had to walk under these kids-only things.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: They decided that orphans were a certain height?

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: I guess so. I mean, I was certainly getting under that. So I'd probably still get under that today.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: By the way, Harley has dwarfism. That's what she meant by that joke. She's 4 foot 6. I pretty quickly got to the point. Why did you walk out that day? And the answer was not what I expected at all. I thought Harley was bombing because of what Barbara Walters said, because she had stage fright. But it wasn't nerves stopping her.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: That's not stage fright. That's frustration that I can't sing. I'm not scared, I'm pissed. Like, I'm mad at myself in that moment.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: (SINGING) You're always a day--

segments.text: A-

segments.text: A-

segments.text: I have no pitch, and the poor man was trying so hard to get me to sing the right note, and I just couldn't do it. Start to get hot. Your hands start to get clammy, your heart starts to race. All these people are now looking at me. And I don't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: Which of course casts her sudden disappearance in an entirely different light.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: It was not a feeling of fear of being on stage, or fear of auditioning. It was just an overwhelming feeling of this not being right for me. Think it was just this isn't what I want to be doing right now. It stopped being fun, and I just looked at both of my parents and I said, I'm done. I don't-- I don't want to do this anymore. I'm ready to go. And there was absolutely no questioning of me on that at all. They said, OK, let's go.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: Were you embarrassed leaving? Did you say goodbye to people? Like, the way it's framed in the show is this very abrupt thing. But how did it feel in the moment? What did it look like?

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: The moment my parents said we could leave, I was comfortable. I was like all right, guys. Let's get out of here. Let's go get a snack.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: Why she didn't stick around that day, it wasn't an act of fear. It was an act of courage.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: I feel like I've always been pretty in tune with myself. And I know when something is not right. And I've done this with other things in my life, where I've gotten pretty far with something, and then I'm like eh, I think we're done.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: So there's this like other little person inside of you.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: Is that a short joke?

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: It wasn't a short joke, but when I said it, I was worried that you might think it is. But it wasn't. So there was, I'm going to start over. So there was a voice in your head speaking to you in a language that you understand, but couldn't quite speak yet.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: But what you were able to interpret in the moment was?

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: This isn't right for me.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: And I don't feel good.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: And I need to get out.

segments.speaker: Harley Ott
segments.text: I need to leave.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: So at 7, Harley understood enough to know she wasn't good enough. She walked away. She felt fine. Me, it took me much longer to figure it out. I auditioned for the 8th grade musical, and didn't get in.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: I auditioned for the 9th grade musical, didn't get in. I auditioned for the 10th grade play, and didn't get in. I tried transferring to Interlochen, an elite arts boarding school for teens. Didn't get in. My senior year of high school, all the kids enrolled in theater were given one song to sing in an end-of-year revue.

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: The teacher gave me an easy one, a song from the musical "Hairspray." About growing up.

segments.text: Harley's a bad singer, but she's obviously got something. She's a good actor. What you don't find out about her in that Barbara Walters special is that she actually went onto a pretty successful child acting career. She starred in a Nick at Nite short, multiple commercials, even a Val Kilmer movie. But me?

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: So OK, Mama. Be honest, OK?

segments.text: You were-- you had talent. But you know, I don't believe you were the star, the big star. You never got the leading role.

segments.text: You loved it, Lina. You loved it. I mean, you loved the musicals. I mean, you were like an encyclopedia. I have a very vivid memory of you going to Borders on your tippy-toes, asking the person behind the desk for the musical "Annie Get Your Gun." And you were telling him you want the 1938. No, it wasn't '38, because in '39 Judy Garland did "Wizard Of Oz."

segments.speaker: Lina Misitzis
segments.text: OK. So I had different talents. Harley says that when acting stopped being fun, she moved on. She's a teacher now in New Jersey. And of course, I've moved on, too. Mostly. Almost entirely. Really, any day now.
